Let’s dive into Chapter 9: Leading Up and Down the Chain of Command.
You know, leadership isn’t just about managing the people who answer to you. It’s also about something called “leading up”—basically, having a positive influence on those above you in the organization.
Here’s the interesting part: no matter where you sit on the org chart, you actually play a part in shaping your team’s direction and success. Sounds empowering, right?
So, what does leading up really look like? Well, first, it’s about providing information that’s clear and to the point. When you give your leaders the facts they need, you help them make better decisions.
It’s also about thinking ahead. If you can anticipate what your boss might need before they even ask, you’re already setting yourself—and your team—up for success.
And let’s be real—everyone runs into problems. But when you bring a challenge to your boss, try to offer a solution too, not just the issue itself. This shows initiative and problem-solving skills, both of which build trust with those above you.
Now, let’s switch gears for a moment. Leading down the chain of command is just as important. For those who report to you, it’s all about clear communication, setting expectations, and making sure they have what they need to get the job done.
Picture this: you’re a middle manager and you spot a problem that keeps slowing your team down. Instead of waiting for senior leaders to notice, you gather some data, come up with a solid solution, and bring it forward proactively. Not only do you help your team, but you also show the higher-ups that you’re reliable and ready to take initiative.
At the end of the day, leading up and down is about building a culture where everyone supports each other and shares responsibility.
When people at every level step up and take ownership, the whole organization gets stronger and more adaptable.
